panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Clinical photograph of a 3-month-old female patient with Saethre-Chotzen syndrome (TWIST1 mutation per in-text) showing significant turribrachycephaly secondary to bicoronal synostosis, as explicitly stated in the caption. Real human-patient image with a specific, captioned SCS manifestation; the visible tall, short cranial shape supports the finding. b: CT volume rendering of the same 3-month-old Saethre-Chotzen syndrome patient demonstrating bicoronal craniosynostosis, a hallmark SCS finding directly stated in the caption. Real patient imaging with clear disease attribution; no skin is assessable on this bone-rendered CT.
panels.attribution_text: Chu et al. CASE REPORT Pan-Suture Synostosis After Posterior Vault Distraction.. Eplasty 2013. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Three-month-old female patient with Saethre-Chotzen syndrome and bicoronal synostosis resulting in significant turribrachycephaly (a). The sagittal, lambdoid, and squamosal sutures were patent with a large fontanelle, characteristic of Saethre-Chotzen syndrome. Initial computed tomographic volume rendering shows bicoronal craniosynostosis (b).
in_text_mentions: Our patient presented at 3 months of age with bilateral coronal synostosis and profound turribrachycephaly (Fig 1). Gene testing was positive for TWIST1 mutation, consistent with Saethre-Chotzen syndrome. She underwent bilateral posterior occipital craniotomy and posterior vault distraction at 6 months of age to lower the cranial high point and expand the anterior-posterior cranial length. Internal distractors with 4-cm distraction arms were placed along the osteotomy sites of the parietal bones; the intended vector was posterior-inferior from the skull apex (Fig 2).
